results.title: CutCat: Skip Mature Content on Netflix in Chrome, Free
results.content: CutCat is a free Chrome extension that mutes or skips mature content, nudity and gore while you watch Netflix. It works from scenes that other viewers have already marked, so the film keeps playing and you simply do not sit through that part. The extension runs inside the Netflix player you already use in Chrome on a computer, and it is not affiliated with Netflix. Its promise is deliberately narrow: keep watching, skip the scene. CutCat is built for people who want to stay with a series or a film but would rather not sit through nudity, gore, strong language, kissing or credits, and who want to decide for themselves which of those categories count. The problem it addresses is a familiar one for anyone watching a title that mixes a story they want with material they do not. A marked scene [...] the coverage is deepest. Breaking Bad leads with 115 scenes marked, followed by Dark on 107, Outlander on 74, Bridgerton on 58, Vikings on 54, Spartacus on 52, Shameless on 45, Castlevania on 44, You on 42, Squid Game on 37 and 13 Reasons Why on 34. Further down the list are Cyberpunk: Edgerunners on 27, The Platform and Bodies on 26 each, UNABOMBER on 25, Troy: Fall of a City and The Witcher on 24, Apex on 22, Captain Fall on 20, Ozark on 19, Colors of Evil: Red and Unfamiliar on 18, The Tudors on 17, Something Very Bad Is Going to Happen and Stranger Things on 16, and American Psycho, Unlocked, The Beast in Me, Black Mirror and Peaky Blinders on 15 each. The list is a snapshot rather than a fixed set. CutCat is best understood as a small, single-purpose tool that does one job in the [...] as a small, single-purpose tool that does one job in the Netflix player and then stays out of the way. It skips or mutes marked scenes, lets the viewer choose which categories apply, keeps settings in the browser, records nothing about what is watched, and costs nothing. The value proposition is the sentence the site opens with: keep watching, skip the scene. Put it on, then forget it is there.

Coming from the age of peak cable TV, I was used to ongoing scripted TV shows releasing seasons every year. They would go on break long enough for me to miss them, but not long enough to forget them either. But Netflix has broken this fine balance. This was painfully obvious with "Shadow and Bone." I loved the first season and was practically ready for the second season right away. The excitement only grew when a second season was announced 45 days later. [...] In an interview with Deadline, Netflix's Chief of Content, Bela Bajaria, said that part of the streamer's strategy is to release shows faster so audiences have something to watch while the rest of the episodes are cooking. She also said that sometimes, it's the creator's choice. "Peter Morgan on 'The Crown,' Shonda Rhimes on 'Bridgerton,' there was a way that they wanted to structure or write it because they felt it was an actual, natural emotional break.
